DOJ subpoenas of journalists and press-freedom risk 5
Subpoenas were hand-delivered to three New York Times reporters at their homes on July 10th over reporting on security weaknesses in the Qatari-donated Air Force One, followed by a second wave of subpoenas to phone carriers covering the reporters' and their relatives' records back to January 1st.

So what: The broad, retroactive scope (reaching back to Jan 1 and to family members) signals a general leak-hunting operation rather than a narrow single-story inquiry, raising the stakes for any organization handling sensitive government information.
A federal judge in the Southern District of New York froze enforcement of the subpoenas pending a hearing after the Times moved to quash them, and the DOJ subsequently agreed to hold the subpoenas in abeyance while pursuing further investigative steps.

Unlike a comparable 2025 search warrant against a Washington Post reporter (tied to an active Venezuela-related leak prosecution), the NYT subpoenas were issued the same day Cash Patel was at the White House on the president's direct request, an unusually fast and personally-directed process for a media leak investigation.

Lawfare Daily: Can State Laws Protect Against Misuse of the National Guard?58 min22 insights2026-07-23
▶ Watch on YouTube
Brennan Center researchers Liza and Joseph, joined by Lawfare senior editor Lauren Voss, discuss their new 50-state compendium of National Guard law, concluding that Title 32/Section 502F deployments (currently active in DC, Tennessee, and Louisiana) evade the federal Posse Comitatus Act because no state has an equivalent statute, that several states have unconstitutional martial-law and mass-arrest statutes still on the books, and that Virginia's new oversight law offers the clearest template for state legislatures to reassert control.
The Legal Architecture of National Guard Deployment · 5The Posse Comitatus Gap at the State Level · 3Unconstitutional and Conflicting State Statutes · 6Reform: Virginia's Model and the Path Forward · 3Elections, Transparency, and Systemic Risk · 5
The Legal Architecture of National Guard Deployment 5
The National Guard operates under three distinct statuses: state active duty (governed by state law, commanded by the governor), Title 10 (federalized, commanded by the president, same status as active-duty military), and Title 32 — a hybrid status where the Guard nominally remains under gubernatorial command while performing a federally funded mission.
framework🗣 Lauren Voss, Lawfare senior editorconviction: highNational GuardTitle 32Title 10
So what: This three-tier framework is the baseline for assessing legal risk in any domestic Guard deployment; investors/analysts tracking political and regulatory risk should identify which status applies before assuming Posse Comitatus protections exist.
Section 502F of Title 32 (specifically the 2006-added subsection 502F(2)(A)) allows a governor to deploy the National Guard to support a federal mission at the request of the president or Secretary of Defense, with almost no statutory text defining the scope of what missions qualify.
framework🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: highSection 502FNational Guard
So what: The vagueness of 502F's text is the specific legal hinge enabling expansive domestic use of the Guard; any future deployment justified under 502F should be scrutinized against its narrow legislative history (disaster response, counter-drug support) rather than its broad literal wording.
Legislative history indicates Congress designed 502F to fund the Guard's traditional disaster-response and counter-drug functions, not to authorize suppression of civil unrest or general crime control, yet the Trump administration has used it for exactly those purposes — starting with 2020 protest deployments (11 states sent Guard to DC after George Floyd's killing) and now for 'crime control' missions in DC, Memphis, and New Orleans.
causal🗣 Liza, Brennan Centerconviction: highSection 502FDonald TrumpWashington DCMemphisNew Orleans
So what: Establishes a repeatable precedent: an administration can invoke 502F for domestic policing missions well outside its original intent, which is a template likely to recur in future administrations regardless of party.
Nearly 5,000 National Guard troops are currently deployed in Washington DC, largely standing idle rather than performing substantive law-enforcement tasks, and President Trump has said the deployment will continue until January 2029 — an open-ended, effectively permanent posture rather than the traditional short-term crisis response.
data_point🗣 Liza, Brennan Centerconviction: highNational GuardWashington DCDonald Trump
So what: Signals a durable shift from emergency-response use of the military to a standing, quasi-permanent domestic military presence — a structural change in US domestic governance with implications for civil-liberties and municipal-cost analysis.
Although Title 32 nominally leaves 'command and control' with the governor, in practice only administrative (paperwork) control stays with the state in the DC deployment — both tactical control (people on the ground) and operational control (mission definition, priorities) run through the DC National Guard and a federal joint task force chain.
thesis🗣 Lauren Voss, Lawfare senior editorconviction: highNational GuardWashington DCTitle 32
So what: Demonstrates that the legal fiction of 'state control' under Title 32 does not match operational reality, undermining any assumption that gubernatorial command meaningfully constrains federal use of deployed Guard forces.
The Posse Comitatus Gap at the State Level 3
No US state or territory has a law equivalent to the federal Posse Comitatus Act, which is a 'clear statement rule' requiring express legislative authorization (not case-by-case approval) before the president can use the military for law enforcement — a gap the Brennan Center's nationwide compendium confirmed is universal.
data_point🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: highNational GuardPosse Comitatus Act
So what: The single most important finding of the compendium: without a state-level equivalent, Title 32 deployments face essentially no analogous federal-style check, making state legislative reform the primary available remedy.
“There is no state that has a law saying that a governor's deployment of the National Guard for law enforcement has to be pursuant to an express statutory authorization.” ▶ 43:18
The Posse Comitatus Act applies only to federal officials and federalized (Title 10) forces, not to state officials or Title 32 National Guard, which is precisely why Title 32/502F has become the preferred legal vehicle for domestic military deployment under this administration.
causal🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: highPosse Comitatus ActTitle 32National Guard
So what: Identifies the specific statutory loophole being exploited, useful for anticipating that any future administration seeking to expand domestic military use will similarly route through Title 32 rather than Title 10.
The historical absence of state-level Posse Comitatus equivalents partly reflects that most state Guard statutes and constitutional provisions predate a major shift in the National Guard's role: since the end of the draft, and especially since the late 1990s and post-9/11, the Guard has been increasingly integrated into combat deployments, with roughly half of Iraq/Afghanistan troops drawn from the Guard/Reserve versus under 1% in Vietnam, and over one million Guard members having done combat tours.
causal🗣 Liza, Brennan Centerconviction: highNational Guard
So what: Undercuts the traditional assumption that the Guard is less suited to combat-style domestic policing than active-duty forces — today's Guard increasingly shares the same training and 'battle mindset' as active duty, raising the stakes of using it domestically without Posse-Comitatus-style constraints.
Unconstitutional and Conflicting State Statutes 6
An Illinois statute (20 Illinois Compiled Statutes) purports to allow the National Guard, when deployed in response to civil unrest, to arrest any person in view without process and detain them indefinitely — a provision Joseph calls unconstitutional on its face under the Fourth, Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments and the right to habeas corpus, yet it remains on the books.
data_point🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: highIllinoisNational Guard
So what: A live, unrepealed statute that could be invoked in a crisis despite being unenforceable — a concrete legal-risk flag for anyone tracking Illinois emergency-powers exposure.
Iowa Code section 29A.46 purports to let the governor set up military tribunals to try civilians in areas placed under martial law, which Joseph says conflicts with the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments and with Supreme Court precedent (Ex parte Milligan, Duncan v. Kahanamoku) holding that even where martial law is otherwise permissible, military trial of civilians is not — and it also conflicts with Iowa's own state constitution.
data_point🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: highIowamartial law
So what: Another concrete, currently-live unconstitutional statute; both the Iowa and Illinois examples show state legislatures have not cleaned up facially unconstitutional emergency-powers law even decades after enactment.
Thirteen states have a statutory-constitutional conflict where the state constitution requires the military be subordinate to civil power, yet a state statute purports to authorize the governor to declare martial law; Tennessee is the starkest example — its constitution explicitly prohibits declaring 'martial rule,' yet a Tennessee statute purports to authorize exactly that.
data_point🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: highTennessee
So what: A specific, checkable list (13 states) of jurisdictions where martial-law statutes are legally void on their face — useful for any legal-risk assessment of a hypothetical martial-law declaration in those states.
No state governor has declared martial law since the governor of Maryland did so in 1963, but many states still retain martial-law-authorizing statutes enacted mostly during the 1861-1945 period — dormant but legally live.
data_point🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: highmartial law
So what: Establishes a long dormancy period that could create false confidence; these statutes remain available tools for a governor willing to test them despite eight decades of disuse.
State law on National Guard 'peace officer' status (the authority to make arrests) varies enormously: Missouri and Arkansas make every Guard member a peace officer by default whenever on duty regardless of law-enforcement training, while other states restrict peace-officer status only to trained military police.
data_point🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: mediumMissouriArkansasNational Guard
So what: A concrete illustration of how uneven state-by-state legal exposure is for Guard members and the public they interact with, relevant to assessing liability and due-process risk by state.
Many states' National Guard laws (Wisconsin and New York are cited examples) are simply vague or underdeveloped, lacking clear deployment criteria, which leaves broad discretion to the governor by default rather than by deliberate design.
data_point🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: mediumWisconsinNew YorkNational Guard
So what: Identifies a first-order reform priority: even before addressing law-enforcement powers, many states need basic statutory clarity on when a governor may deploy the Guard at all.
Reform: Virginia's Model and the Path Forward 3
The Brennan Center's core reform recommendation is for states to enact their own 'mini Posse Comitatus Acts' that flip the default from broad gubernatorial discretion to requiring the Guard be used for law enforcement only pursuant to specific statutes enacted by the state legislature — not a ban on Guard law-enforcement use, but a requirement that legislatures, not governors alone, define its scope.
framework🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: highNational GuardPosse Comitatus Act
So what: A specific, actionable legislative template that state lawmakers in any state could adopt now, giving a concrete benchmark for grading future state legislative sessions on Guard oversight.
Virginia's recently enacted HB86 is held up as a partial model: it requires the Adjutant General to submit an annual report on the Virginia Guard's status, federal funding, and use by federal authorities; it slightly narrows the governor's deployment authority; it reinforces existing prohibitions on using the Guard for election interference; and it creates a working group to study further reforms.
data_point🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: highVirginiaNational Guard
So what: A concrete, already-passed legislative template other states can copy verbatim or adapt, making it the most immediately trackable benchmark for state-level Guard oversight reform.
Tennessee is one of the few states where existing state law actually constrained a Guard deployment: a lower court found the Memphis Guard deployment violated Tennessee's own statutory limits, though that ruling is currently stayed pending appeal.
data_point🗣 Liza, Brennan Centerconviction: mediumTennesseeMemphisNational Guard
So what: Proof-of-concept that state law can function as a real check where it exists and is specific enough — a live case to monitor as a bellwether for whether state courts will enforce these limits against a federally directed mission.
Elections, Transparency, and Systemic Risk 5
The primary federal restriction on troops at polling places, 18 U.S.C. 592, bars both the military and 'federal civil officers' from polling sites — meaning that even a Title 32 deployment nominally under gubernatorial command could still trigger liability under 592 if the president or Secretary of Defense directed it as a federal mission.
framework🗣 Lauren Voss, Lawfare senior editorconviction: mediumNational Guardelections
So what: Clarifies that the 'state command' framing does not necessarily shield a Title 32 deployment from election-related legal exposure, an important nuance for assessing 2026 midterm deployment risk.
Separate from 592, both state and federal voter-intimidation laws apply to anyone regardless of deployment authority or intent, depend only on effect (not intent), and — unlike 592 — can be enforced through private lawsuits, making them the more practical backstop against Guard involvement in intimidating voters.
framework🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: highNational Guardelections
So what: Identifies the most enforceable legal remedy available if Guard forces are used near polling places in 2026, relevant for anyone assessing election-integrity risk.
Both guests describe a severe, current lack of public transparency about which legal authority (Title 10, Title 32, or state active duty) governs any given National Guard deployment and what its mission scope actually is, making real-time legal or legislative oversight extremely difficult.
thesis🗣 Liza, Brennan Centerconviction: highNational Guard
So what: Identifies a structural information gap that itself is a policy target — greater mandatory disclosure of deployment legal authority and mission scope (as Virginia's law begins to require) would materially improve accountability.
Guard members deployed on open-ended domestic missions are pulled away both from their civilian jobs (teachers, healthcare workers, shopkeepers) and from the military training and readiness they would otherwise be doing for foreign-threat response, a hidden cost to both their home communities and national defense readiness.
causal🗣 Joseph, Brennan Centerconviction: highNational Guard
So what: A second-order cost of prolonged domestic deployments — lost military readiness and community labor capacity — that is rarely counted in the public debate over these deployments' benefits.
Guard members are generally not well trained in the legal distinctions between arrest and detention, creating downstream due-process complications for anyone they detain — illustrated by a specific example of a Guard detention near the Dupont Circle Metro station in DC.
anecdote🗣 Lauren Voss, Lawfare senior editorconviction: mediumNational GuardWashington DC
So what: A concrete illustration of practical legal risk (weak criminal cases, civil-liability exposure) created by using undertrained military personnel for law-enforcement-adjacent tasks.

Raise Act Substance & Legislative Evolution 3
The Raise Act as passed required frontier AI labs to publish and adhere to a public safety plan and report 'critical safety incidents' to government; earlier drafts also barred releasing a model that failed the developer's own safety tests and required independent third-party audits, but both of those provisions were stripped after lobbying before the governor signed the final version.

After Governor Hochul signed the Raise Act while publicly criticizing its compliance burden, a subsequent chapter amendment converted it from something closer to a liability regime into more of a transparency regime, which Bores acknowledges as both true characterizations depending on perspective.
data_point🗣 Alex Boresconviction: highRaise ActKathy HochulNew York

The number of qubits believed necessary to solve certain useful quantum computing problems has fallen roughly 100x over the past five years, from an estimated ~1 million qubits down to roughly 10,000, due to improved algorithms and error-correction schemes.

Three scenarios for Chinese AI governance -- and the models' own self-assessment 8
The ChinaTalk team modeled three scenarios for how Beijing handles a frontier-capable ('mythos-level') Chinese model: 'Let It Rip' (status quo -- models release with no real pre-release safety review, and a bad incident becomes the forcing function for policy change), 'Black Box' (the state takes a lab's most capable model in-house for government/offensive use rather than letting it release openly), and 'Glasswing' (an evaluate-before-release process, with capabilities lobotomized before public release, modeled on an existing playbook already referenced in industry).

So what: Gives investors and policymakers a concrete three-way scenario tree for forecasting Chinese frontier-model release policy, useful for scenario-weighting export-control and open-weight-diffusion risk.

What CLARITY actually does for token classification 3
The bill designates all tokens as commodities by default but layers a securities-style disclosure regime (audited financials, use-of-proceeds, management team disclosures) onto tokens classified as 'ancillary assets' — those raised via fundraising to build something — making it, according to Miller, the most disclosure-heavy digital asset bill proposed to date, more so than the Digital Commodity Exchange Act or the DCCPA.

Tokens like Bitcoin fall into a separate 'network token' category that can exit disclosure obligations entirely by passing a two-part test: first a decentralization/lack-of-control test, then an efforts test showing the original fundraiser is no longer engaged in more than nominal ongoing entrepreneurial or managerial activity.

The bill explicitly protects developers performing only technical infrastructure roles — running a validator, operating a node, creating an oracle service, or simply providing a user interface — from securities and commodities exchange act registration requirements.

The Epic Fury AI-enabled targeting program represents a leapfrog in applying AI to the military targeting-and-fires process, cutting through the fog of war to strike before an adversary can respond, but current capability shown publicly still has another 10x-100x of improvement ahead as AI models and infrastructure advance.

How Franchise Restaurants Opened the Door to the Gig Economy | Odd Lots48 min16 insights2026-07-24
▶ Watch on YouTube
Open Markets Institute chief economist Brian Callaci, author of 'Chains of Command: The Rise and Cruel Reign of the Franchise Economy,' explains to Tracy Alloway and Joe Weisenthal how a 1960s-70s antitrust-law rewrite let franchisors like McDonald's control nearly every aspect of a 'franchisee's business while offloading employer liability, how that same legal architecture underpins today's Uber and Amazon gig-worker classification, and how wage suppression remains the one lever franchisees can pull.
Franchise structure and the principal-agent problem · 3The 1960s-70s antitrust rewrite that legalized franchisor control · 3Empirical evidence on franchise wages · 3From franchising to the gig economy · 3Policy, private equity, and the regulatory pendulum · 4
Franchise structure and the principal-agent problem 3
A franchise is legally simple: the franchisor licenses its trademark to a nominally independent franchisee for a royalty (typically 6-20% of sales), while dictating nearly every operational detail -- prices, hours, product mix, even how many seconds an employee has to greet a customer and which approved equipment (e.g., McDonald's ice cream machines) they may use -- making franchisees functionally 'middle managers with more risk' rather than true independent business owners.
framework🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highMcDonald'sfranchisingtrademark law
So what: Undercuts the 'entrepreneurship' marketing narrative used to recruit franchisees and gig workers -- a useful lens for evaluating any 'be your own boss' investment or labor-supply pitch.
“a franchise or just like an entrepreneur makes the worst franchisee.” ▶ 0:20
Franchising partly solves the principal-agent problem (an owner-operator with 'skin in the game' works harder than a salaried manager), but Callaci argues its bigger historical appeal to franchisors was legal: franchisees are classified as separate businesses rather than employees, so they don't qualify for overtime or minimum-wage protections and, until recently, had no clear legal path to unionize against the parent brand.
causal🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highfranchisinglabor lawprincipal-agent problem
So what: Highlights franchising as fundamentally a labor-cost-arbitrage legal structure, relevant to evaluating labor-cost and regulatory risk in any franchise-heavy public company.
The primary, and often only, lever a franchisee has to improve unit profitability is squeezing labor costs, because the franchisor controls nearly everything else, including staffing levels mandated in the operations manual, which the franchisor can unilaterally change at any time.
thesis🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highfranchisingwagesMcDonald's
So what: Direct investment implication: franchise-model profitability at the unit level is structurally tied to wage suppression, making labor-cost regulation (minimum wage hikes, joint-employer rules) a first-order risk factor for franchisors and franchisees alike.
“the major lever that franchisees have, to be a better business to produce more money is to basically squeeze wage costs.” ▶ 0:00
The 1960s-70s antitrust rewrite that legalized franchisor control 3
Franchisor control over pricing, territory, and products was illegal under 1960s-70s antitrust law, which treated it as an anti-competitive vertical restraint incompatible with the 'independent business owner' model; founders like Ray Kroc and Colonel Sanders, together with the newly formed International Franchise Association, ran a deliberate, self-acknowledged lobbying and litigation campaign -- aided by University of Chicago law-and-economics scholars -- to redefine antitrust doctrine so this control became legal under a 'rule of reason' standard.
causal🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highantitrust lawInternational Franchise AssociationUniversity of ChicagoRay KrocColonel Sanders
So what: Traces the specific legal-doctrine shift underlying today's platform and gig-economy legal architecture -- relevant background for assessing regulatory-reversal risk to gig and franchise business models.
In 1963 and 1965 Senate Antitrust Subcommittee hearings, the International Franchise Association's own president effectively conceded, under questioning, that franchisors sought 'vertical integration by other means' -- wanting full operational control without the legal liabilities of actually owning the business or employing the workers.
data_point🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highInternational Franchise AssociationSenate Antitrust Subcommittee
So what: An original-source, citable historical admission of franchisor intent, useful for legal and regulatory risk analysis around misclassification litigation theories.
“we're trying to get vertical integration by other means. We don't want to own the assets. We don't want to employ the workers. Those are risks we'd rather do without. We want the benefits of that control, but we really don't want to be held liable for it.” ▶ 14:20
Franchise contracts historically included no-poaching clauses preventing workers at one location of a brand from being hired by another location of the same brand without the current franchisee's permission -- legal under antitrust's vertical/horizontal distinction (a franchisor-imposed no-poach is treated more leniently under 'rule of reason' than an illegal horizontal agreement between competitors) even though its wage-suppressing effect is economically identical.
causal🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highno-poach agreementsantitrust lawMcDonald's
So what: Flags a well-documented anti-competitive labor practice that has drawn state attorney general and DOJ scrutiny in recent years -- relevant precedent for assessing labor-antitrust litigation risk in franchise-heavy sectors.
Empirical evidence on franchise wages 3
Callaci's research, exploiting a natural experiment where Washington state entered a consent decree with McDonald's and other chains eliminating no-poach clauses, found wages rose afterward -- a causal empirical finding that no-poach restrictions measurably suppressed franchise-worker wages.
data_point🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highWashington stateMcDonald'sno-poach agreements
So what: Direct empirical evidence quantifying the wage impact of eliminating anti-competitive labor clauses -- relevant to modeling margin impact if similar consent decrees or FTC rules expand nationally.
Research cited by Callaci (David Weil's 'The Fissured Workplace' and earlier work by Alan Krueger) finds that even within the same brand, workers at company-owned locations earn higher wages and have better long-term wage/promotion trajectories than workers at franchised locations of the identical chain, and franchised locations have measurably higher rates of workplace-safety and other labor-law violations.
data_point🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highDavid WeilThe Fissured Workplace
So what: A concrete, sourced wage and violation gap between corporate-owned and franchised units -- a useful comparative metric for labor-risk screening of franchise-heavy restaurant and retail companies.
Callaci and colleagues hand-coded 530 franchise contracts over 18 months, drawing on public records made available under a 1979 FTC rule requiring franchise disclosure documents filed in certain states like Wisconsin and California; follow-up research using text-scraping tools has since found franchise contracts have become measurably more restrictive over the past 20 years.
data_point🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highFederal Trade Commissionfranchise disclosure document
So what: Identifies an underused public-record dataset (state-filed FDDs) and a documented, worsening trend in contractual restrictiveness -- a leading indicator for labor-cost and regulatory risk in franchise-sector investments.
From franchising to the gig economy 3
Callaci argues the legal architecture gig-economy platforms like Uber and Amazon's 'Delivery Service Partner' program use to classify workers as independent contractors is a direct descendant of the franchise antitrust victories of the 1960s-70s, arguing Amazon's DSP model is even closer to a franchise than Uber, since DSP operators are small incorporated companies (running, say, 30 trucks) rather than individual driver-entrepreneurs, with Amazon reportedly fronting some capital while keeping drivers legally employed by the DSP rather than by Amazon.
causal🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highAmazonUberDelivery Service Partnersgig economy
So what: A direct legal-lineage argument connecting franchise case law to gig-platform liability shielding -- relevant for assessing misclassification and liability litigation risk at Amazon, Uber, or similar platforms.
Unlike a traditional vertically-integrated manufacturer such as 1950s US Steel or General Motors, which had comparatively less granular real-time control over its own directly-employed workforce, McDonald's today -- despite employing hardly anyone directly -- exercises tighter operational control over its franchisees via continuous point-of-sale and broadband data feeds since the 1990s, and now AI-based worker-level surveillance able to flag a specific slow employee by name to the franchisee.
thesis🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highMcDonald'sUS SteelGeneral MotorsAI surveillance
So what: Highlights how real-time data and AI dramatically increase the degree of practical operational control corporations can exert without a formal employment relationship -- an important framework for evaluating 'control without liability' risk in any modern platform business, not just restaurants.
“McDonald's now hardly employs anybody, but they have way more control because they're able to get that, that stream of data.” ▶ 26:43
Domino's imposes a 30-minute delivery guarantee that pressures drivers to speed, yet if a driver rushing to meet that corporate-mandated deadline causes an accident, liability legally falls on the franchisee or driver rather than Domino's corporate.
anecdote🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highDomino's
So what: A concrete illustrative case of 'control without liability' exposure -- relevant precedent for tort and liability-risk analysis in franchise and delivery-driven business models.
Policy, private equity, and the regulatory pendulum 4
Callaci's proposed policy fix is not to ban franchising or centralized corporate control -- he acknowledges real efficiency benefits from coordinated, centrally-planned corporate structures -- but to tie legal employer obligations and liabilities directly to whichever entity exercises real operational control, regardless of contractual labels.
framework🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highfranchisingjoint employerlabor policy
So what: A clear, actionable regulatory framework that, if adopted via new joint-employer rules or legislation, would directly raise labor costs and liability exposure for franchisors and gig platforms -- relevant for scenario-planning regulatory risk in these sectors.
Historically, private equity primarily bought franchise brands themselves -- the capital-light, high-margin, royalty-collecting franchisor entity, with Burger King cited as a famous example -- but Callaci notes a newer trend of private equity also acquiring and consolidating franchise operator businesses, including multi-unit and even multi-brand franchisee groups.
data_point🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: mediumprivate equityBurger Kingfranchisees
So what: Flags a structural shift worth tracking for restaurant-sector PE investors: growing consolidation of franchisee operating companies (not just franchisor brands) changes labor-cost and consolidation dynamics at the unit-operator level.
Under the 1947 Taft-Hartley Act, franchise workers are legally barred from striking, picketing, or targeting the franchisor corporation directly and can only target their 'immediate employer' (the local franchisee); a 2010s Obama-era 'joint employer' NLRB rule briefly made it easier for workers to compel franchisor-level bargaining, but it was rescinded under Trump, restored under Biden, then reversed again, leaving the legal status of franchise-worker collective bargaining unsettled today.
data_point🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highTaft-Hartley Actjoint employer ruleNational Labor Relations Board
So what: Flags the 'joint employer' rule status as a specific, binary, politically-toggled regulatory variable that materially changes franchisor labor-cost and liability exposure depending on the administration in power -- a recurring pendulum to track at each administration change.
Contrasted with franchised chains like Dunkin' Donuts and Taco Bell, fully corporate-owned chains like Starbucks and Chipotle pay measurably higher wages and have allowed workers to at least vote for unionization (Starbucks) in ways franchise workers structurally have not, suggesting some of the rents generated by centralized corporate control can be shared with workers when the parent company is the direct employer.
contrarian🗣 Brian Callaci, chief economist, Open Markets Instituteconviction: highStarbucksChipotleDunkin' DonutsTaco Bell
So what: Gives a clean comparison set (corporate-owned vs. franchised chains) investors and analysts can use to benchmark labor-cost and union risk differences within the restaurant sector.

Institutional custody technology reaching retail 3
Since roughly 2019-2020, institutional crypto custodians (Copper, Fireblocks, BitGo, Anchorage, Coinbase Custody) have not actually generated or stored a single private key for client wallets -- instead using MPC (multi-party computation) to create wallets as pre-split key shares requiring a threshold of shares (e.g., 2-of-3) to sign a transaction, a technology gap retail wallets like MetaMask and Ledger have not adopted.
data_point🗣 Dimitri Tokarev, founder Bron Walletconviction: highCopperFireblocksBitGoAnchorageCoinbaseMetaMaskMPC
So what: Identifies a specific, multi-year technology gap between institutional and retail crypto custody that a new wallet entrant is explicitly built to close -- useful context for evaluating custody-risk exposure across different wallet providers.
“Private keys are not being created in institutional space... it's absolutely not the case [that institutions write down 24-word seed phrases]” ▶ 5:46
Bron Wallet, founded in 2025 after raising $15 million, is explicitly repositioning MPC-based institutional custody technology for retail, high-net-worth, and family-office users who cannot justify paying the roughly $500,000-600,000 annual fees charged by full institutional custodians like Copper, BitGo, Fireblocks, or Anchorage for a smaller (e.g., ~$5 million) pool of assets.

Physical coercion ('wrench attacks') against crypto holders has become frequent enough -- occurring roughly every couple of months by the founder's account, including people he personally knows -- that wallet providers are now explicitly designing programmable defenses against it, rather than treating it as a rare tail risk.

Bron Wallet lets users program transaction security delays (e.g., 2-72 hours) and multi-party approval thresholds (e.g., three approvers required above $250,000, five above $1 million) so that no single compromised or coerced individual can unilaterally move large sums, directly targeting both organized fraud and physical duress scenarios.

The larger a centralized crypto platform's asset pool becomes, the more attractive a target ('honeypot') it becomes for sophisticated state-linked hacking groups like Lazarus, citing Bybit's ~$1.5 billion hack in February 2025, which the exchange was only able to absorb because it happened to have sufficient reserves to reimburse users.
